topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the Same World through Different Eyes

sections.title: The Hook: The Tale of Two Navigators
sections.content: Introduce a scenario where two characters, Alice and Bob, are navigating the same terrain but using different maps. Alice uses a standard North-East grid (Standard Basis), while Bob uses a grid aligned with a tilted mountain range (Basis B). Establish that they are looking at the same 'Point P' but have different coordinates for it.
sections.example: Alice says the treasure is at (3, 2). Bob, standing on his tilted grid, says it's at (1, 1). Who is right? Both are! They are just using different 'languages' or bases.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Briefly define a basis as a set of 'unit' vectors that act as building blocks. In 2D, any point can be reached by a combination of two non-parallel vectors. Visualize the standard basis i (1,0) and j (0,1) as a clean square grid.
sections.example: Animation: Show a vector [3, 2] being constructed by 3 steps of i and 2 steps of j. Then, swap the grid to two diagonal arrows to show a new 'custom' grid being formed.

sections.title: The Translation Matrix (The 'Dictionary')
sections.content: Explain that to understand Bob, Alice needs to know what Bob's basic 'steps' (basis vectors b1 and b2) look like in her world. We arrange Bob's basis vectors as columns in a matrix. This matrix P is our 'Dictionary' or Change of Basis Matrix.
sections.example: If Bob's first step b1 looks like (2, 1) to Alice, and his second step b2 looks like (-1, 1) to Alice, the matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]].

sections.title: The Core Formula: Mapping Coordinates
sections.content: Present the fundamental equation: [v]_Alice = P * [v]_Bob. Explain that multiplying Bob's coordinates by matrix P 'translates' them into Alice's standard coordinate system. Use a visual of Bob's grid morphing and stretching to align with Alice's square grid.
sections.example: If Bob says a bird is at (1, 1) in his system, Alice calculates: [[2, -1], [1, 1]] * [1, 1]^T = [1, 2]. Alice sees the bird at (1, 2) in her standard system.

sections.title: Going Backwards: The Inverse Matrix
sections.content: What if Alice wants to tell Bob where the bird is? We need the Inverse Matrix (P^-1). Explain that [v]_Bob = P^-1 * [v]_Alice. This allows for two-way communication between different viewpoints.
sections.example: Alice sees a cloud at (4, 2). By multiplying by the inverse of P, she can tell Bob exactly where to look on his tilted map.

sections.title: Visual Summary and Application
sections.content: Summarize that a Change of Basis is simply a linear transformation that reinterprets coordinates. Mention real-world applications like computer graphics (camera vs. world space) or JPEG compression (pixel space vs. frequency space).
sections.example: Animation: A 3D camera moving through a forest. As the camera (Bob) rotates, the trees (Points) stay the same in the world (Alice), but their coordinates relative to the camera change constantly via basis transformation.
